I ran the numbers twice before I let myself believe them. The relay had been quiet
for two days.

Boro had come in from Kepler on the morning shuttle, still smelling of vault
sealant, and he sat down across from me without being asked.

"You heard about Vela," he said.

I had. The Vela relay was destroyed by the Quiet, and the news of it had sat in my
chest for a week like a swallowed stone. Cyra had logged eleven minutes of it
before the carriers dropped.

"I heard," I said. "I also heard you sealed the Kepler vault."

"Nine hours." He turned his hands over. "And then last autumn I found the second
cradle empty, which is a thing I would rather not have found."

Cyra arrived a little after that, straight off the Vela packet, and she had the
drift lanes with her — the whole map beyond Vela, mapped and measured, the thing
she had been promising for years.

The Ledger Stone sat on the table between us where Boro had put it down. It looked
smaller out of the cradle. It always does.

"Thule has stopped answering the long channel," Cyra said. "Has done for years."

"Dael is dead," I said. "The breach took the whole garden section."

Dael pushed the tomatoes across the table anyway, because Dael has never once let
a fact interfere with a gesture.

The lattice came online after that and abolished the signal delay, and it changed
everything, and none of us said very much for a while.

The console at Sol threw up the same answer either way. The console at Sol threw
up the same answer either way, and the console at Sol threw up the same answer
either way, and I began to wonder whether the console at Sol threw up the same
answer either way because it was broken or because I was.

Outside the port, the traffic lanes were doing their slow arithmetic. The traffic
lanes were doing their slow arithmetic and the slow arithmetic was doing the
traffic lanes, and the traffic lanes were doing their slow arithmetic still.
